genre/jungle-en-drum-and-bass.text: In the early 1990s London producers sped up the breakbeats of rave to 160 to 180 bpm and put a deep, slow bass line under them, borrowed from reggae and dub: jungle. In the mid-1990s the style became tighter and more technical and acquired the name drum and bass, with Goldie, Roni Size and LTJ Bukem as well-known names.
genre/jungle-en-drum-and-bass.listen: Listen to Inner City Life for the fast, broken drums set against the calm vocals and the long chords.

genre/k-pop.text: K-pop is South Korean pop music that grew from 1992, when Seo Taiji and Boys sang hip hop and rock in Korean. Big entertainment companies train young artists for years in singing, dancing and presentation and put groups together from them, with teams of songwriters and producers from home and abroad. That idea of a team turning out hits at a rapid pace had appeared earlier with Stock Aitken Waterman and Max Martin. With Dynamite (2020), BTS became the first Korean act to reach number 1 in the Billboard Hot 100.
genre/k-pop.listen: Listen to Dynamite for the tight disco groove and the vocals shared out among the members of the group.

genre/kabuki-en-shamisen.text: In 1603 Izumo no Okuni performed with her dance troupe in the dry bed of the Kamo river in Kyoto, and that is regarded as the beginning of kabuki. Where Noh is sober, kabuki is colourful and spectacular. The music revolves around the shamisen, a three-string lute with a skin-covered soundbox, which came from China via the Ryukyu Islands. In the eighteenth century nagauta grew out of it, literally long song: singing with shamisen, flute and drums.
genre/kabuki-en-shamisen.listen: Listen to this shamisen solo from Dōjōji for the way the strings are struck hard and dry with a large plectrum.

genre/kansas-city-jazz.text: Under the rule of the corrupt politician Tom Pendergast, Kansas City remained an open city in the 1920s and 1930s: clubs ran all night, even during Prohibition and the Depression. Musicians from all over the Southwest flocked to it and played endless jam sessions. The music was built strongly on the blues and revolved around the riff, a short repeated motif that a section plays behind a soloist. Many arrangements were not written down but devised together from memory: head arrangements. Bennie Moten led the most important orchestra; after his death in 1935 the pianist Count Basie started a band of his own, with the tenor saxophonist Lester Young. Andy Kirk with Mary Lou Williams, Jay McShann with the young Charlie Parker, and the singer Big Joe Turner with the pianist Pete Johnson also came out of this scene.
genre/kansas-city-jazz.listen: Find the riff: a short motif that keeps coming back behind the soloist.

genre/karnatische-muziek.text: The classical music of South India took shape in the sixteenth century in Vijayanagara, present-day Hampi, where Purandara Dasa wrote the exercises with which students still begin today. As in the north, everything revolves around raga, a scale with fixed turns, and tala, a rhythmic cycle, but here the composed song, the kriti, is central. Around 1800 Tyagaraja, Dikshitar and Syama Sastri wrote the classics of the repertoire. Violin and mridangam, a double-headed drum, accompany the voice.
genre/karnatische-muziek.listen: Listen to how M.S. Subbulakshmi, in this song by Purandara Dasa, plays around the notes of raga Kapi with undulating ornaments, gamakas.

genre/keelzang-van-toeva-en-mongolie.text: On the steppes of Tuva and Mongolia, herders have been singing two notes at once for centuries. The singer holds a low fundamental note and, with throat, tongue and lips, shapes the overtones above it into a whistling melody. There are different styles: khoomei sounds soft, sygyt high and whistling, kargyraa deep and growling. The Tuvan group Huun-Huur-Tu, founded in 1992, combines these voices with the igil, a bowed instrument with strings of horsehair, and brought throat singing to stages all over the world.
genre/keelzang-van-toeva-en-mongolie.listen: Listen to the voice in Kongurei: can you hear a sustained low note beneath the melody, and sometimes a whistling overtone above it?

genre/klankmassa-s-xenakis-ligeti-en-pen.text: Around 1955 composers let go of melody and wrote with sound masses: clouds of dozens of voices that each do something slightly different, so that you hear only the whole. Iannis Xenakis, an architect with Le Corbusier, calculated the gliding strings of Metastaseis with mathematics; the piece was premiered in Donaueschingen in 1955. In Atmosphères (1961), György Ligeti had an orchestra slowly shift in colour, and Krzysztof Penderecki wrote his Threnos for the victims of Hiroshima (1960) for 52 strings.
genre/klankmassa-s-xenakis-ligeti-en-pen.listen: Listen to Atmosphères and notice that there is no melody and no beat: dozens of instruments play notes lying right next to one another, and the sound slowly changes colour, like a cloud.

genre/klassieke-televisiemuziek.text: Television called for short, instantly recognisable music. A tune had to set the tone within a few seconds and return every week. Bernard Herrmann wrote the first title music for The Twilight Zone (1959); the well-known guitar riff by Marius Constant followed a season later. The Doctor Who tune (1963) was written by Ron Grainer and turned into electronic music by Delia Derbyshire of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, using oscillators and spliced tape. For Mission: Impossible (1966), Lalo Schifrin wrote a theme in 5/4 time. Jan Hammer made the music for Miami Vice (1984) with synthesizers and scored a number 1 hit with it. Angelo Badalamenti gave Twin Peaks (1990) a dreamy, slow synthesizer sound.
genre/klassieke-televisiemuziek.listen: Notice how short the theme is and what makes it instantly recognisable: an unusual time signature, an electronic sound or a single guitar figure.

genre/kleinkunst.text: Kleinkunst is the Dutch-language song from cabaret and theatre, with the lyrics at the centre and a small accompaniment; in the 1950s Wim Sonneveld, Toon Hermans and Jules de Corte were the big names. Around 1965 that tradition shifted towards pop, when Boudewijn de Groot sang songs to lyrics by Lennaert Nijgh, inspired by American folk and Bob Dylan. In the 1980s Klein Orkest brought kleinkunst to a pop band.
genre/kleinkunst.listen: Listen to Over de muur for how a narrative song about East and West Berlin arrives at a chorus that everyone sings along to.

genre/klezmer.text: The klezmorim, Jewish professional musicians, already had a guild of their own in Prague in the sixteenth century and later played throughout Eastern Europe. Their most important work was the Jewish wedding, which lasted for days: music for the processions, to listen to at the table and to dance to. Violin, clarinet, brass and the hammered dulcimer tsimbl played a repertoire with roots in synagogue chant, the Baroque and Ottoman music. Emigrants such as Naftule Brandwein and Dave Tarras took it with them to New York.
genre/klezmer.listen: In this recording from 1923, Naftule Brandwein plays clarinet in the orchestra of Abe Schwartz. Notice how he ornaments the melody with trills, slides and little sobs.

genre/koreaanse-nieuwe-golf.text: Around 2000 South Korean film acquired an international voice of its own. Directors such as Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon-ho mixed genres and often had music work against the image. In Oldeuboi (2003), waltzes and strings from the team of the composer Jo Yeong-wook accompany violence and revenge, so that the scenes become almost balletic. For Ah-ga-ssi (2016), Jo wrote a warm orchestra with Baroque touches. For Gisaengchung (2019), Jung Jae-il wrote music that sounds like a Baroque suite while a poor family infiltrates a rich household. For the series Ojing-eo geim (2021) he chose childlike sounds, such as the recorder and simple rhythms. What they have in common is irony: elegant music accompanying cruel events.
genre/koreaanse-nieuwe-golf.listen: Listen to how an ornate waltz or Baroque figure simply carries on while the tension on screen rises: the contrast between music and action is the message.

genre/kraftwerk-en-de-mens-machine.text: Kraftwerk was founded in Düsseldorf in 1970 and left guitar and drum kit behind for synthesizers, electronic drums and the vocoder. Autobahn (1974) opens with a 22-minute track about a drive along the motorway; Trans-Europe Express (1977) sounds like wheels on rails. The influence extended to hip hop in New York and techno in Detroit.
genre/kraftwerk-en-de-mens-machine.listen: Listen to Trans-Europe Express for the tight rhythm without swing, like a train on the rails.

genre/krautrock.text: In West Germany, bands such as Can, Neu! and Kraftwerk sought a sound of their own, free of American and British rock; English journalists called it krautrock. Neu! was founded by Michael Rother and Klaus Dinger, who had played briefly with Kraftwerk. Their motorik beat later returned in post-punk, in electronic music and with Radiohead.
genre/krautrock.listen: Listen to Hallogallo for how the drums keep the same 4/4 rhythm for minutes on end without fills, like a car at a constant speed.

genre/krontjong.text: Krontjong arose in Batavia, present-day Jakarta, out of songs that Portuguese sailors brought with them from the sixteenth century onwards. Small string instruments, which resemble the ukulele, play an undulating rhythm beneath a highly ornamented vocal line, with flute, violin and cello alongside. In the 1920s and 1930s krontjong became popular throughout Indonesia via radio and film; Gesang's Bengawan Solo (1940) became a classic. After 1949 Indo-Dutch people took the music with them to the Netherlands, where it became one of the roots of indorock.
genre/krontjong.listen: Listen to Bengawan Solo for the undulating accompaniment of the small string instruments beneath the calm singing.

genre/kulintang.text: Kulintang is a row of five to nine bronze knobbed gongs lying on a wooden frame. Among the Maguindanao and Maranao on Mindanao and the peoples of the Sulu archipelago, it is the core of an ensemble with large hanging gongs, the agung and gandingan, and the drum dabakan. The music is heard at weddings and festivals, and it is often regarded as an instrument for women. European travellers described the centuries-old tradition as early as the sixteenth century.
genre/kulintang.listen: José Maceda recorded this Maguindanao player in 1955 in Dulawan, Cotabato. Listen to the melody on the row of gongs: can you hear how a short pattern keeps returning, ornamented differently each time?

genre/laatromantiek.text: Around 1900 orchestras, symphonies and emotions grew to gigantic proportions. Gustav Mahler, director of the Court Opera in Vienna from 1897, wrote symphonies of more than an hour in which marches, folk songs and heartfelt adagios stand side by side. In symphonic poems such as Also sprach Zarathustra (1896), Richard Strauss told an entire story with the orchestra alone. Their harmony stretched the key so far that the next generation let go of it.
genre/laatromantiek.listen: Listen to how in Zarathustra a trumpet climbs above a low organ note and the whole orchestra, with timpani, builds to an enormous climax.

genre/latin-jazz.text: From 1943 Machito and Mario Bauzá mixed jazz with Cuban music in New York. In 1947 Dizzy Gillespie took the Cuban conga player Chano Pozo, who had recently moved to New York, into his big band. Jazz swings long-short, while Afro-Cuban music is built on evenly divided notes and the clave; in Latin jazz the two come together. From 1958 João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim created bossa nova in Rio de Janeiro.
genre/latin-jazz.listen: Listen to Manteca for Pozo's conga ostinato and a bebop bridge in swing: two rhythmic worlds in one piece.

genre/latin-trap.text: Latin trap is trap in Spanish, from Puerto Rico. De La Ghetto and Arcángel were already rapping over trap beats around 2007, but around 2016 it became a wave, via SoundCloud and YouTube. You hear the 808 bass and rattling hi-hats of trap from Atlanta, with the language and sometimes the rhythm of reggaeton. Bad Bunny broke through in 2016 with Soy Peor and Anuel AA with Sola. In 2018 I Like It by Cardi B, Bad Bunny and J Balvin reached number one in America.
genre/latin-trap.listen: Listen to Sola for the slow beat with the deep 808 bass and fast hi-hats beneath the Spanish vocals.

genre/levenslied-en-smartlap.text: The levenslied is the Dutch-language song about love, sorrow, mothers and the city, with a simple melody that everyone can sing along to. Its roots lie with the street singers and the smartlappen, songs full of drama. In the 1950s the Amsterdam Jordaan became the centre, with Johnny Jordaan and Tante Leen, and in the 1980s André Hazes made the levenslied big.
genre/levenslied-en-smartlap.listen: Listen to Geef mij maar Amsterdam for the waltzing accompaniment and the lyrics singing the praises of the singer's own city.

genre/live-begeleiding-bioscooppianist-o.text: Silent films were never silent. From the first screenings around 1895 a pianist played along, later in large halls a theatre organ or a whole orchestra. The musician improvised or chose pieces from a library of short, characteristic fragments: a ‘hurry’ for chases, a ‘misterioso’ for suspense, an ‘agitato’ for quarrels or danger. From 1913 the publisher Sam Fox brought out such collections, with music by John Stepan Zamecnik. Film companies sent cue sheets along: lists that indicated for each scene what kind of music was suitable and how long it had to last. In this way a shared language of musical clichés arose. Sound film later largely took over that language.
genre/live-begeleiding-bioscooppianist-o.listen: Notice how each piece establishes a single mood or action in a few bars, so that a pianist or orchestra could play it under any film.

genre/lofi-hiphop.text: Lo-fi hip hop is calm, instrumental hip hop to study or relax to. Lo-fi stands for low fidelity: the sound is deliberately a little dull, with the hiss and crackle of an old record. The beats are slow and sound slightly sloppy, with samples of jazz piano and guitar. Major examples were the Japanese producer Nujabes and the American J Dilla. From 2017 the French YouTube channel ChilledCow, now Lofi Girl, made the genre world-famous with a livestream that runs day and night.
genre/lofi-hiphop.listen: Listen to Time: The Donut of the Heart for how J Dilla turns a snippet of soul by The Jackson 5 into a slow, slightly dragging loop.

genre/madrigaal.text: In Florence in the 1520s and 1530s, northern composers such as Philippe Verdelot and Jacques Arcadelt wrote part-songs on Italian poems, often in the spirit of Petrarch. This is how the madrigal arose, for four or five singers who let every word be heard. Sighs, tears and dying received a sound of their own, with grating harmonies and sudden silences. With Monteverdi and Gesualdo, the madrigal became ever more dramatic around 1600.
genre/madrigaal.listen: In Arcadelt's Il bianco e dolce cigno, about a swan that dies singing, listen to how the four voices mostly sing the same syllables together, so that you can understand every word, and how, at the closing line about dying a thousand times, they enter one after another.

genre/mambo.text: The mambo grew out of the danzón and the son in Havana in the late 1930s. From 1949 the pianist and bandleader Dámaso Pérez Prado made it a craze in Mexico City, with a big band that had the brass play sharp and high. In the early 1950s thousands of people in New York also danced the mambo, including at the Palladium Ballroom.
genre/mambo.listen: Listen to Mambo No. 5 for the fierce trumpets, the saxophones playing against the beat and the cries of Pérez Prado.

genre/maori-waiata-en-haka.text: When Polynesian seafarers reached Aotearoa, present-day New Zealand, between 1250 and 1300, they brought their art of singing with them. Waiata are sung songs. The old mōteatea include lullabies, laments and love songs, and pass on knowledge from generation to generation. The haka is a dance with shouts, stamping feet and fierce facial expressions. The best known, Ka Mate, was composed by the chief Te Rauparaha around 1820. Both forms live on in kapa haka groups.
genre/maori-waiata-en-haka.listen: This recording from 1952 lets you hear the haka of Te Rauparaha. Notice the leader and the group's response: how do they use rhythm, breath bursts and shouts instead of melody?

genre/mariachi-en-son-jarocho.text: In the nineteenth century, small groups with violins, harp and guitars such as the vihuela played in western Mexico, especially in Jalisco around Cocula: the mariachi. The word is older than the French occupation of the 1860s, so the well-known explanation via the French mariage is not correct. In 1908 the Cuarteto Coculense made the first recordings, and later trumpets were added. Meanwhile on the Gulf Coast the son jarocho grew up, with jarana, requinto and harp and dancers on a wooden platform.
genre/mariachi-en-son-jarocho.listen: In this recording from 1926, listen to how the violins carry the melody and the guitars strike the rhythm. Is there already a trumpet, as in later mariachi music?

genre/marsmuziek-en-brassbands.text: In the late nineteenth century nearly every American town had a brass band, and John Philip Sousa, leader of the United States Marine Band in Washington, wrote marches such as The Stars and Stripes Forever (1896). A march is in 2/4, with the emphasis on 1 and 3, and consists of several melodies one after another, the strains. Ragtime took over that time signature and form, and in New Orleans brass bands played at funerals: a slow hymn on the way to the cemetery, cheerful music on the way back.
genre/marsmuziek-en-brassbands.listen: Listen to The Stars and Stripes Forever for the tight beat in two and the melodies that alternate, as later in ragtime.

genre/mbira.text: Thumb pianos with iron tongues have sounded in the Zambezi Valley for some 1,300 years, and in 1586 the Portuguese missionary João dos Santos described one. Among the Shona in Zimbabwe, the mbira dzavadzimu, the mbira of the ancestors, became the sacred instrument of the bira: nocturnal ceremonies in which players, together with hosho rattles, summon the ancestors. In the 1970s the mbira became a symbol of the struggle for independence, and Thomas Mapfumo translated its patterns to the electric guitar.
genre/mbira.listen: Nhemamusasa is one of the best-known mbira pieces of the Shona. Listen to how short patterns are repeated endlessly and yet always seem to sound different, because the parts interlock.

genre/mento.text: Mento is the folk music of the Jamaican countryside, played on banjo, guitar and the rumba box, a large thumb piano on which the bass sounds. In the 1950s mento was first put on record, often with double-entendre lyrics. Mento was sometimes called calypso, but it is a style of its own. It is one of the roots of ska.
genre/mento.listen: Listen to the banjo, the guitar and the deep notes of the rumba box in the light, skipping rhythm.

genre/merengue.text: Merengue is the national dance of the Dominican Republic: fast music in 2/4 with accordion, the tambora, a double-headed drum, and the güira, a metal scraper. In the 1930s, under the dictator Trujillo, the merengue became the country's official dance music. In the late 1980s Juan Luis Guerra took it, with jazz and pop influences, to an international audience.
genre/merengue.listen: Listen to Ojalá Que Llueva Café for the fast rhythm of tambora and güira beneath the part-singing.

genre/mesopotamie.text: In the royal tombs of Ur, in the south of present-day Iraq, Leonard Woolley found lyres with a golden bull's head around 1929. They were made around 2500 BC and are the oldest surviving stringed instruments. More than a thousand years later, a hymn to the goddess Nikkal was written down in cuneiform at Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, with Babylonian instructions for a nine-string lyre. It is the oldest nearly complete music in writing that we know.
genre/mesopotamie.listen: This is a reconstruction of the Hurrian hymn, played on a rebuilt lyre. Listen to how the melody circles in small steps around a few central notes, and bear in mind that the scale and the rhythm have been filled in by researchers.

genre/minimal-music.text: In the 1960s American composers made music out of short patterns that are repeated endlessly and change slowly. Terry Riley wrote In C (1964), in It's Gonna Rain (1965) Steve Reich had two tape loops slowly drift out of step, and Philip Glass worked with repeated arpeggios; he and Riley were inspired by Indian music. Minimal music became a source for ambient, techno and electronic music, and for bands such as The Velvet Underground.
genre/minimal-music.listen: Listen to Music for 18 Musicians for how short patterns are repeated again and again and change step by step.

genre/minimal-music-in-film.text: Minimal music arose in New York in the 1960s: music made from short patterns that are repeated again and again and slowly altered. In 1982 Philip Glass brought that principle to film with Koyaanisqatsi, a film without dialogue or story, in which image and music do the work together. In the same year the Briton Michael Nyman wrote energetic music on bass lines by Henry Purcell for Peter Greenaway's The Draughtsman's Contract. Nyman later scored The Piano (1993), Glass The Hours (2002), among others. Clint Mansell used the technique with the Kronos Quartet in Requiem for a Dream (2000). Repetition gives movement without telling the image what it should feel.
genre/minimal-music-in-film.listen: Notice a single short pattern that keeps returning and how small changes in rhythm or harmony build tension.

genre/minstrelshows.text: From the 1830s white performers with blackened faces appeared in minstrel shows: blackface performances in which Black Americans were ridiculed, with songs, dances and sketches that supposedly came from life on the plantation. The stock character Jim Crow later gave his name to the laws that kept Black and white people separate. The minstrel show was also the first major form of popular entertainment in America: the banjo found its way into white music through these shows, songwriters such as Stephen Foster wrote for them, and after the Civil War Black performers appeared as well. It is a painful origin, but one that shows how intertwined the traditions were.
genre/minstrelshows.listen: There is deliberately no recording here. Read in the reader how the banjo made its way into country music through these shows.

genre/modale-jazz.text: In modal jazz the musicians do not improvise over a fast series of chords, but for a long time over a single mode: a scale with a character of its own, such as Dorian. That gives more room to think melodically. In 1953 the composer George Russell described the idea in his theory book on the Lydian concept. Miles Davis applied it on Milestones (1958) and on Kind of Blue, recorded in March and April 1959 in the Columbia studio on 30th Street in New York. The opening piece, So What, has sixteen bars in D Dorian, eight bars a semitone higher and eight again in D. Kind of Blue became the best-selling jazz album ever. In the 1960s John Coltrane, the pianist McCoy Tyner and Herbie Hancock built on the modal approach.
genre/modale-jazz.listen: Notice how long the accompaniment stays on one harmony and how the soloist fills that space.

genre/moderne-r-en-b.text: The term rhythm and blues came back as R&B: vocals, production and drum machines are central, and the producer becomes a star. The beginning lies with Michael Jackson and Quincy Jones; Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis brought Prince's Minneapolis sound to Janet Jackson (Control, 1986). Via new jack swing and hip hop soul, R&B and hip hop became the core of the mainstream after 2000.
genre/moderne-r-en-b.listen: Listen to I Wanna Dance with Somebody for a gospel voice in a synth-pop production.

genre/modernisme-atonaliteit-en-avant-ga.text: From the mid-1950s the language of modern concert music came into film. Leonard Rosenman, who had studied with Arnold Schönberg, wrote East of Eden (1955) and The Cobweb (1955). The latter is often regarded as Hollywood's first twelve-tone score. In Planet of the Apes (1968), Jerry Goldsmith used twelve-tone rows, a great deal of percussion and wind instruments played with unusual techniques. For 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), Stanley Kubrick chose existing works by György Ligeti, and for The Shining (1980) music by Ligeti and Krzysztof Penderecki. In this way clusters, glissandi and atonality became the sound of fear, the unknown and space.
genre/modernisme-atonaliteit-en-avant-ga.listen: Notice the planes of sound and clusters without a clear melody, and the instruments played in an unusual way.

genre/moog-en-de-eerste-synthesizerpop.text: From 1964 Robert Moog built synthesizers in Trumansburg that a musician could play himself, with an ordinary piano keyboard. Wendy Carlos made the instrument known with Switched-On Bach (1968), and in 1970 the portable Minimoog appeared. Hot Butter's Popcorn (1972) became a worldwide hit, with the synthesizer as a funny sound on top of an ordinary band.
genre/moog-en-de-eerste-synthesizerpop.listen: Notice that the synthesizer in Popcorn plays only one note at a time: the first synthesizers were monophonic.

genre/moombahton.text: In late 2009 the DJ Dave Nada was playing at a party for his cousin in Washington. The guests wanted to hear reggaeton, so he slowed down a Dutch house track, Afrojack's remix of Moombah, from about 128 to 108 bpm. That is how moombahton arose, a name from Moombah and reggaeton. The tempo is slow, the rhythm is the dembow of reggaeton and the sounds come from Dutch house. In 2015 Major Lazer took the sound into the charts with Lean On.
genre/moombahton.listen: Listen to Que Que for the slow, swaying dembow rhythm beneath the hard synthesizers of Dutch house.

genre/motown.text: In 1959 Berry Gordy started a label in Detroit that he organised like a car factory, with regular songwriters, the house band The Funk Brothers and a weekly quality-control meeting. The aim was Black music that white audiences would buy as well: 'The Sound of Young America'. The Supremes scored twelve number 1 hits; in 1972 Motown moved to Los Angeles.
genre/motown.listen: Listen to the tambourine on the beat and the nimble bass line of James Jamerson.

genre/muziek-van-papoea-nieuw-guinea.text: Papua New Guinea has hundreds of languages and at least as many musical styles. The kundu, an hourglass drum with a head of lizard skin, even appears in the national coat of arms. The garamut, a hollowed-out tree trunk, is a slit drum for music and for messages that carry for miles. At a singsing, song, dance, feasting and gifts come together. Among the Kaluli in the rainforest, voices deliberately sing just beside and over one another, like the sounds of the forest.
genre/muziek-van-papoea-nieuw-guinea.listen: Steven Feld recorded this in the rainforest of Bosavi, during the felling of trees for a new garden. Can you hear how voices, working sounds and the forest mingle? Do the voices sing exactly together, or just beside and over one another?

genre/nationale-scholen.text: Outside Germany and Italy, composers in the nineteenth century sought a national sound of their own, with folk songs, dance rhythms and stories from their country. In 1862 a free music school was founded in Saint Petersburg, where Mily Balakirev formed The Five with Mussorgsky, Borodin, Rimsky-Korsakov and Cui. In Vltava (1874), Bedřich Smetana painted the river through Bohemia, and Edvard Grieg wrote music for Ibsen's play Peer Gynt. Dvořák and Sibelius, among others, followed later.
genre/nationale-scholen.listen: Listen to how in Vltava undulating lines in the strings depict the flowing water, while a broad melody lets the river sing.

genre/nederbeat.text: Around the Beatles' visit in June 1964, beat bands sprang up all over the Netherlands, with The Hague as the centre: the Golden Earrings, Q65, the Motions and Shocking Blue. Almost all of them sang in English; Cuby + Blizzards played heavy blues from Grolloo. In February 1970 Shocking Blue's Venus became the first Dutch record to reach number 1 in the Billboard Hot 100.
genre/nederbeat.listen: Notice the simple guitar riff of Venus and the chorus that you can sing along to after hearing it once.

genre/nederhop.text: From 1990 Osdorp Posse of Amsterdam began rapping in broad Amsterdam dialect: hardcore rap about the street and the city. In 1995 Extince of Oosterhout scored the first Dutch-language hip hop hit with Spraakwater. After 2000 Nederhop grew into one of the country's most important genres, with De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig and Typhoon, among others.
genre/nederhop.listen: Listen to Spraakwater for how smoothly Dutch rhymes and swings over a relaxed funk beat.

genre/nederlandse-en-vlaamse-filmmuziek.text: In the Netherlands and Flanders, the feature film acquired a face of its own from the 1960s. In 1966 the director André Delvaux and the composer Frédéric Devreese began their collaboration with De man die zijn haar kort liet knippen. The arranger and composer Rogier van Otterloo worked with Paul Verhoeven on Turks Fruit (1973) and Soldaat van Oranje (1977). He combined a large string orchestra with jazz soloists, such as the harmonica player Toots Thielemans in Turks Fruit. The Flemish conductor and composer Dirk Brossé wrote a romantic orchestral score for Stijn Coninx's Daens (1992). Verhoeven later worked with the British composer Anne Dudley on Zwartboek (2006). Melody and light music play a large role.
genre/nederlandse-en-vlaamse-filmmuziek.listen: Notice the combination of a broad string orchestra with a soloist from jazz or light music.

genre/nederlandse-trance.text: Around 2000 trance became a Dutch export product. DJs such as Tiësto, Armin van Buuren and Ferry Corsten played all over the world, and in 2004 Tiësto played at the opening of the Olympic Games in Athens. ID&T organised Sensation in the Amsterdam ArenA.
genre/nederlandse-trance.listen: Notice the long build-up to the moment when the beat drops back in.

genre/nederpop.text: Nederpop is the collective name for Dutch pop music. In the early 1980s bands broke through that sang in their own language, the Dutch counterpart of the Neue Deutsche Welle. Doe Maar played ska and reggae with Dutch lyrics and broke through massively in 1982; Het Goede Doel made synth-pop and the Frank Boeijen Groep new wave. Singing in Dutch now became ordinary pop in the charts too.
genre/nederpop.listen: Listen to Sinds 1 dag of 2 (32 jaar) for the ska rhythm with the guitar on the offbeat.

genre/neo-soul.text: Neo-soul is R&B that harked back to the soul of the 1970s, with Erykah Badu and D'Angelo, among others. Badu recorded Tyrone (1997) live, with harmonies from jazz, and the warm sound of the Rhodes piano also reappeared. On her solo album (1998), Lauryn Hill combined doo-wop choirs, a soul groove and rap.
genre/neo-soul.listen: Notice that Tyrone was recorded live, with jazz harmonies beneath the voice.

genre/neoclassicisme.text: After the First World War, composers looked back at the clarity of the eighteenth century, but with a modern eye. In 1917 Sergei Prokofiev wrote a symphony of the kind Haydn would have written in his own day. For the ballet Pulcinella (1920, with sets by Picasso), Stravinsky adapted melodies attributed to Pergolesi and gave them modern rhythms and sharp harmonies. Ravel honoured the French Baroque with Le tombeau de Couperin.
genre/neoclassicisme.listen: Listen to the Sinfonia of Pulcinella for a Baroque melody, and notice the dry winds and small shifts that betray that this is 1920.

genre/neoprog.text: Neo-prog arose in England around 1981, when progressive rock had gone out of fashion. Young bands such as Marillion, IQ, Pallas, Pendragon and Twelfth Night took early Genesis and Camel as their example, but played with the energy and sound of the 1980s: shorter songs, glossy synthesizers and a singer who played a role on stage. Marillion of Aylesbury became the biggest. The concept album Misplaced Childhood (1985) reached number 1 in England, and Kayleigh reached number two.
genre/neoprog.listen: Listen to Kayleigh for how the guitar carries the melody with a clear, echoing sound, while Fish sings his lyrics like a letter to a lost love.

genre/neotraditionele-jazz-young-lions.text: In the early 1980s a generation of young musicians emerged who wanted to return to acoustic jazz, with swing, blues and hard bop as a basis. The trumpeter Wynton Marsalis of New Orleans played with Art Blakey in 1980 and then signed with Columbia. In 1984 he won Grammys in both jazz and classical music. Together with his brother, the saxophonist Branford Marsalis, and musicians such as Terence Blanchard, Donald Harrison, Roy Hargrove and Joshua Redman, he was counted among the Young Lions: well-dressed young players who took the tradition seriously. Record companies actively looked for such talent. From 1987 Marsalis worked on the jazz programme of Lincoln Center in New York. Critics accused the movement of fixing the history of jazz as a set canon and of excluding fusion and free jazz.
genre/neotraditionele-jazz-young-lions.listen: Listen to the swing of the rhythm section: the language of the 1950s, played by twenty-somethings.

genre/neue-deutsche-welle.text: Around 1979 a wave of German-language rock and pop arose in West Germany out of punk and new wave, which the journalist Alfred Hilsberg called Neue Deutsche Welle. It began in the avant-garde with DAF and Einstürzende Neubauten and within a few years ended up in the charts. The Austrian Falco also scored in this wave, with Der Kommissar. By around 1985 the genre had disappeared.
genre/neue-deutsche-welle.listen: Listen to how 99 Luftballons sounds cheerful and yet is a protest song against the Cold War.

genre/new-hollywood.text: In the late 1960s young directors in Hollywood gained more freedom. Their films were more personal and rawer, and the music changed along with them. Sometimes it came from pop music, sometimes from a sober, European corner. The Italian Nino Rota gave The Godfather (1972) a melancholy waltz that begins with a lonely trumpet. For Chinatown (1974), Jerry Goldsmith chose a small, unusual line-up with solo trumpet, strings, pianos and harps. Bernard Herrmann completed the music for Taxi Driver (1976) shortly before his death, with a languid saxophone theme and menacing brass. In this period the score more often became a sparse colour than a large, continuous carpet.
genre/new-hollywood.listen: Notice how a single solo instrument, a trumpet or saxophone, carries the loneliness of the main character.

genre/new-jack-swing.text: In the late 1980s, the producer Teddy Riley in New York combined the singing of R&B with the beats of hip hop: new jack swing. The drum machine swings, with a short, hard snare, while singers such as Bobby Brown and Keith Sweat sing soulfully over it. In the early 1990s hip hop soul grew out of new jack swing.
genre/new-jack-swing.listen: Listen to My Prerogative for the swinging drum machine and the hard snare beneath Bobby Brown's vocals.

genre/new-orleans-jazz.text: Around 1900 jazz grew out of the brass bands in New Orleans, later also called Dixieland or hot jazz. Cornet, clarinet and trombone improvise at the same time above banjo, tuba and drums: collective improvisation. In 1917 the first jazz record appeared, by the white Original Dixieland Jass Band.
genre/new-orleans-jazz.listen: Follow the division of roles: the cornet plays the melody, the clarinet decorates above it and the trombone slides beneath.

genre/new-romantic.text: In the London club Blitz in the late 1970s, you only got in if you looked striking. Out of that scene came New Romantic, a movement within new wave that leans on glam rock, with make-up, historical costumes and gender bending. Duran Duran made expensive videos and stood at the start of the Second British Invasion via MTV.
genre/new-romantic.listen: Listen to Fade to Grey for the whispered French phrases above a pulsing sequencer bass.

genre/new-wave.text: New wave is a collective name for musicians who wanted to go further after punk, with more attention to atmosphere, melody and sound. The roots lie with punk, but also with disco and krautrock. The movement runs from guitar bands such as The Cure, The Police and The Smiths to synth bands such as Tubeway Army and Depeche Mode.
genre/new-wave.listen: Listen to Are 'Friends' Electric? for the Minimoog and Polymoog: one of the first British number 1 hits in which the synthesizer plays the leading role.

genre/nieuwe-jazz-uit-los-angeles.text: Around 2010 a scene grew up in Los Angeles in which jazz, hip hop and electronic music blend into one another. The producer Flying Lotus, a great-nephew of Alice Coltrane, founded the label Brainfeeder in 2008. The bassist Thundercat, the saxophonist Kamasi Washington and other musicians who already knew each other from school played as the collective The West Coast Get Down. Many of them played on Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly (2015). In the same year Washington released The Epic, an album of nearly three hours with big band, choir and strings, which referred to the spiritual jazz of the 1960s. Thundercat combines virtuoso bass playing with singing and humour. In this way jazz in Los Angeles found a new, young audience through hip hop.
genre/nieuwe-jazz-uit-los-angeles.listen: Listen to the layers: a hip hop beat beneath, jazz improvisation above.

genre/nieuwe-latijns-amerikaanse-cinema.text: Around 2000 a new generation of Latin American directors attracted international attention. Alejandro González Iñárritu, Alfonso Cuarón, Guillermo del Toro and Walter Salles mixed local stories with big themes and often worked outside Hollywood. The Argentine composer Gustavo Santaolalla became the best-known voice of this wave. He himself plays the ronroco, a small Andean lute, and allows a great deal of silence. His music for Amores perros (2000), Diarios de motocicleta (2004) and Babel (2006) sounds intimate and spacious. He won an Oscar for Babel. For El laberinto del fauno (2006), Javier Navarrete by contrast wrote a fairy-tale orchestral score built around a lullaby. Together they show that a small line-up and folk instruments can say as much as a large orchestra.
genre/nieuwe-latijns-amerikaanse-cinema.listen: Notice the thin, metallic sound of the ronroco and how long Santaolalla lets a single note ring before the next one comes.

genre/nieuwe-londense-jazz.text: Around 2015 a jazz scene of musicians in their twenties emerged in London, often with roots in the Caribbean or West Africa. Many of them learned to play at Tomorrow's Warriors, a free training programme for young musicians that the bassist Gary Crosby and Janine Irons founded in 1991. The saxophonist Shabaka Hutchings played in Sons of Kemet, with tuba and two drummers, and in The Comet Is Coming. The saxophonist Nubya Garcia, the tuba player Theon Cross, the drummer Moses Boyd and the band Ezra Collective formed the core of the scene. In 2018 Gilles Peterson released the compilation album We Out Here. The music mixes jazz with grime, Afrobeat, calypso and dub and is played for a dancing audience. In 2023 Ezra Collective became the first jazz group to win the British Mercury Prize.
genre/nieuwe-londense-jazz.listen: Listen to how tuba or bass takes over the role of a bass guitar in dance music.

genre/no.text: Noh is the classical music theatre of Japan, with masked actors, a chorus and a small ensemble. In 1374 the young shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu saw a performance by Kan'ami and his son Zeami and became their patron; Zeami then wrote dozens of plays and the theory of the genre. The ensemble, the hayashi, consists of the nohkan, a bamboo flute, and three drums. The drummers let out long cries between their strokes, and these belong to the music just as much.
genre/no.listen: In Hagoromo, listen to what happens between the drum strokes: the players' long cries help to shape the rhythm.

genre/noorse-hardingfele.text: The Hardanger fiddle is a Norwegian violin with extra sympathetic strings beneath the fingerboard, which vibrate along without the bow touching them. The oldest known one, the Jaastad fiddle of 1651, comes from Ullensvang in Hardanger. Fiddlers played dances there such as the springar, gangar and halling, but also lydarslåttar: pieces to listen to alone. Edvard Grieg was inspired by this music in his Slåttar, Opus 72.
genre/noorse-hardingfele.listen: Knut Buen plays a gangar that goes back to the legendary fiddler Myllarguten. Grieg arranged the same dance for piano. Can you hear a soft resonance sounding along behind the melody? Those are the sympathetic strings.

genre/northern-soul.text: In clubs in the north of England, such as the Twisted Wheel in Manchester and the Wigan Casino (1973–1981), young people danced all night to fast American soul from the 1960s, often obscure singles that had sold little in America. DJs searched fanatically for rare records. The journalist Dave Godin coined the name northern soul in 1970. Gloria Jones's Tainted Love (1964) was one such record; Soft Cell later made a synth-pop hit out of it.
genre/northern-soul.listen: Listen to Tainted Love for the fast tempo and the handclaps that people danced to in the clubs.

genre/nouvelle-vague.text: In the late 1950s young French film critics started making films themselves: cheap, on location and free in form. The music became freer too. For Louis Malle's Ascenseur pour l'échafaud, Miles Davis improvised the music with his group in December 1957 while the images were projected. Martial Solal wrote jazz for À bout de souffle (1960). Georges Delerue worked for François Truffaut, on Jules et Jim among others, and for Jean-Luc Godard. His sad string theme interrupts Le mépris (1963) again and again. With Jacques Demy, Michel Legrand made Les parapluies de Cherbourg (1964), a film in which all the dialogue is sung.
genre/nouvelle-vague.listen: Notice how short pieces of music sometimes begin and stop abruptly, as commentary on the image rather than as background.

genre/nu-jazz.text: In London from the late 1980s, DJs such as Gilles Peterson played acid jazz: jazz, funk and soul for the dance floor. Hip hop producers searched old jazz, soul and funk records for breaks to sample; in 1993 Us3 made Cantaloop on a sample of Herbie Hancock. Out of that meeting between jazz and club culture came nu jazz: an electronic form of jazz, combined with house, downtempo and breakbeat.
genre/nu-jazz.listen: Listen to So Flute for how a jazz flute plays over a house beat.

genre/nu-metal.text: Nu metal is metal combined with hip hop and electronics. Korn of Bakersfield released the first album in this style in 1994; around 2000 nu metal became popular. Linkin Park of Los Angeles had two vocalists: Chester Bennington sang and screamed, Mike Shinoda rapped. That rock was mixing with hip hop was a sign of what was to come.
genre/nu-metal.listen: Listen to Numb for how heavy guitars go together with an electronic beat and synthesizers.

genre/nwobhm-en-thrash-metal.text: In the 1980s heavy metal became harder and faster. In England the New Wave of British Heavy Metal emerged around 1980, with Iron Maiden as the best-known band; in California Metallica made thrash metal, with downpicking. With the producer Bob Rock, Metallica became radio-friendly in 1991.
genre/nwobhm-en-thrash-metal.listen: Listen to Run to the Hills for the galloping rhythm of bass and drums and the two guitars playing side by side in thirds.

genre/oost-europese-nieuwe-golven.text: Around 1960 young directors in Poland and Czechoslovakia made films that broke away from socialist realism. In Poland jazz played a large role, partly because it was regarded as Western and free. The pianist Krzysztof Komeda wrote the music for Roman Polański's Nóż w wodzie (1962) with a small jazz group. He followed Polański to Hollywood for Rosemary's Baby (1968), with a lullaby that Mia Farrow sings herself. In Czechoslovakia, Zdeněk Liška wrote idiosyncratic scores, such as for Marketa Lazarová (1967), with choirs and archaic, almost medieval sounds. Typical features are small line-ups, improvisation and a dark, ironic tone.
genre/oost-europese-nieuwe-golven.listen: Notice the intimate sound of a small ensemble and the space and silence between the sounds.

genre/operette-en-de-wals.text: The operetta was light, comic music theatre with spoken dialogue, dances and songs to sing along to. Jacques Offenbach opened his own little theatre in Paris in 1855 and in 1858 had a success with Orphée aux enfers, a caricature of the gods with a wild cancan. In Vienna the waltz king Johann Strauss II wrote Die Fledermaus in 1874, and in 1905 Franz Lehár made a worldwide success with Die lustige Witwe. In this way the operetta became a forerunner of the musical.
genre/operette-en-de-wals.listen: Listen to how the galop from Orphée aux enfers races along at a furious tempo in two beats: this is the music of the cancan.

genre/organum-en-de-notre-dameschool.text: Around the building of Notre-Dame in Paris, at the end of the twelfth century, singers placed new, mobile voices above a stretched-out Gregorian melody. Léonin collected such two-part pieces, called organum, in a large choirbook. Pérotin even wrote for four voices, as in Viderunt omnes, probably for Christmas 1198. To make the voices move together they used fixed rhythmic patterns, and thus began the polyphony that would shape Western music.
genre/organum-en-de-notre-dameschool.listen: In Pérotin's Viderunt omnes, listen to how the lowest voice holds a single note for a very long time, while three voices above it move in a dancing, constantly repeated rhythm.

genre/ottomaanse-klassieke-muziek.text: At the court of the sultans in Istanbul, an art music of its own grew out of Persian, Arab and Byzantine influences, and acquired its own character in the seventeenth century. It is built on makam, modes with fine intermediate pitches, and usul, long rhythmic cycles struck on drums. Around 1700 the Moldavian prince Dimitrie Cantemir wrote down hundreds of pieces in a notation of letters that he devised himself. The tanbur, a lute with a very long neck and many frets, became the instrument par excellence.
genre/ottomaanse-klassieke-muziek.listen: In this taksim by Tanburi Cemil Bey, recorded more than a hundred years ago, listen to how the tanbur explores the makam with long-ringing notes.

genre/oud-china-klokken-en-hofmuziek.text: At the court of the Zhou dynasty, from around 1100 BC, every ritual was accompanied by music of bronze bells, stone chimes and drums. The most famous example came to light in 1978 in Hubei: the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng, buried in 433 BC, with 65 bronze bells on a wooden rack. Each bell gives two notes, depending on where you strike it, and the note names are cast into them.
genre/oud-china-klokken-en-hofmuziek.listen: This recording was played on a replica of the bells of Marquis Yi; the melody is a modern arrangement. Listen to how each bell sounds short and clear and quickly dies away, and how the low and high bells together make a melody.

genre/oud-egypte.text: On reliefs in tombs near Saqqara, the cemetery of Memphis, harpists, flautists and singers sit side by side around 2500 BC. A singer seems to indicate the melody with hand gestures, and others clap the beat. In the temples, women singers shake the sistrum, a metal rattle associated with the goddess Hathor. The Egyptians did not write music down, so every performance today is a reconstruction on rebuilt instruments.
genre/oud-egypte.listen: This is a reconstruction by Rafael Pérez Arroyo with rebuilt instruments. Listen to how harp, flute and rattles sound together, and ask yourself which choices the musicians had to make themselves because no notes exist.

genre/oud-griekenland.text: In Greece, music, poetry and dance belonged together. Singers accompanied themselves on the lyre or the larger kithara, and the aulos, a double reed pipe, sounded at plays and sacrifices. According to tradition, Pythagoras discovered around 530 BC that the octave and the fifth are simple ratios of string lengths. The Greeks also had a musical notation, with which the Seikilos song has been preserved on a gravestone from the first century: the oldest complete piece of music that we know.
genre/oud-griekenland.listen: This is the Seikilos song, sung to the notes on the stone; rhythm and accompaniment are reconstruction. Listen to how the short melody makes an arc in four phrases, to a text that says you should shine as long as you live, for life lasts only a short while.

genre/palestrina-en-de-romeinse-school.text: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina directed the choirs of major churches in Rome and for a time sang in the papal chapel. The Council of Trent wanted church music that was edifying and kept the text intelligible. Palestrina wrote masses in which the voices move smoothly and dissonances are carefully prepared, such as the Missa Papae Marcelli, printed in 1567. According to a later legend he thereby saved polyphony, and his style remained for centuries the model of pure church music.
genre/palestrina-en-de-romeinse-school.listen: In the Kyrie of the Missa Papae Marcelli, listen to how six voices glide over one another in long, calm lines, without jolts or sharp dissonances.

genre/pansori.text: Pansori is Korean narrative singing by a single singer, the sorikkun, with only a drummer, the gosu, beside them. It arose in the seventeenth or eighteenth century in the southwest of Korea, and a complete story can last for hours. The singer narrates, sings and plays all the roles with a raw, hoarse voice, while the drummer and the audience call out encouraging cries, chuimsae. Of the original twelve stories, five remain, including Chunhyangga.
genre/pansori.listen: In this farewell scene from Chunhyangga, listen to how Eun Hee-jin sings with a hoarse, powerful voice and how the drum sparingly marks the beat.

genre/parallelle-cinema-bengalen.text: In Kolkata in 1955, Satyajit Ray made Pather Panchali, influenced by Italian neorealism. It was the beginning of parallel cinema: films without the songs and stars of Bombay. For the Apu trilogy, the sitar player Ravi Shankar wrote music based on ragas. Vilayat Khan (Jalsaghar, 1958) and Ali Akbar Khan (Devi, 1960) also worked for Ray. From Teen Kanya (1961) Ray wrote his film music himself, including for Charulata (1964). He knew Western classical music well and combined it with Bengali folk music and songs by Rabindranath Tagore. The music is sparing and leaves plenty of room for silence and natural sound.
genre/parallelle-cinema-bengalen.listen: Notice the sitar and the raga melody that builds slowly, and the silences between the music.

genre/peking-opera.text: In 1790 four theatre companies from the province of Anhui came to Beijing for the eightieth birthday of the Qianlong Emperor. Out of their style, later mixed with that of Hubei, Peking opera grew: singing, speech, acrobatics and mime in a single performance. The high, shrill jinghu, a two-string fiddle, leads the singing and percussion marks every movement. Mei Lanfang, famous for his female roles, toured the United States in 1930, and since 2010 Peking opera has been intangible heritage with UNESCO.
genre/peking-opera.listen: In Farewell My Concubine, listen to how the high jinghu follows Mei Lanfang's singing voice closely.

genre/perzische-klassieke-muziek.text: Already around 600 the poet and musician Barbad sang at the Sasanian court of King Khosrow II, but almost nothing of his music has survived. Persian classical music today is organised in twelve dastgahs: modal systems that each consist of dozens of short melodies, gushehs. In the nineteenth century Mirza Abdollah recorded this entire repertoire, the radif. Singers such as Mohammad-Reza Shajarian improvise on classical poetry, accompanied by tar, setar, santur or kamancheh.
genre/perzische-klassieke-muziek.listen: In this daramad, the opening of a dastgah, listen to how Shajarian sings freely and without a beat, and how Mohammad-Reza Lotfi's tar answers his phrases.

genre/philly-soul.text: In Philadelphia the songwriters and producers Kenneth Gamble and Leon Huff made their own soul from the late 1960s, and in 1971 they founded Philadelphia International Records. In Sigma Sound Studio, the house band MFSB recorded lush soul, with strings, horns and a tight, danceable groove. The O'Jays scored with Love Train (1972), and MFSB's TSOP (1974) became the theme tune of the TV programme Soul Train. The Philly sound became one of the building blocks of disco.
genre/philly-soul.listen: Listen to Love Train for the strings and the horns above a groove that keeps rolling.

genre/pinpeat.text: On the reliefs of Angkor Wat, built in the twelfth century, there are already instruments that closely resemble those of the present-day pinpeat ensemble. It is named after the pin, a harp from India that later disappeared from the orchestra. Today it features xylophones (roneat), two gong circles (kong vong), the oboe-like sralai, drums and small cymbals. The centuries-old ensemble accompanies royal dance, shadow theatre and Buddhist ceremonies.
genre/pinpeat.listen: The pinpeat of the royal ballet begins here with Sathukar, the opening piece of every performance. Follow the xylophone roneat ek: does it play the same melody as the gong circle, or does it play around it with faster notes?

genre/pixar-en-digitale-animatie.text: Toy Story (1995) was the first feature-length film animated entirely by computer. For it, Pixar deliberately chose music with a human, warm sound. Randy Newman wrote songs and a score with American roots: honky-tonk piano, swing and a touch of Copland. Later the studio worked with more composers. In Finding Nemo (2003) and WALL-E (2008), Thomas Newman used unusual instruments and small tone colours. For The Incredibles (2004), Michael Giacchino wrote a big band score that recalls spy films of the 1960s. For Up (2009) he won an Oscar, with a simple waltz that tells an entire marriage in the opening montage. At Pixar, music often carries the emotion that the images show without words.
genre/pixar-en-digitale-animatie.listen: Listen to 'Married Life': a single waltz melody is orchestrated differently each time, from playful to fragile, as the couple's life passes by.

genre/polyfonie-van-centraal-afrika.text: In the rainforests in the southwest of the Central African Republic, the BaAka (Aka) sing a centuries-old polyphonic music that has never been written down. Everyone sings along, in four voices that move around one another, and each singer constantly varies their part, so that the song never sounds the same twice. The songs belong to the hunt, to mourning and to the opening of a new camp. From 1971 the musicologist Simha Arom unravelled how this polyphony works.
genre/polyfonie-van-centraal-afrika.listen: Epanda is an invocation of the spirits of the ancestors. Try to follow one voice: how long can you do it before another voice pulls your ear away?

genre/poolse-jazz.text: In Poland around 1950, jazz was regarded as suspect American music. Musicians played in cellars and in people's homes, and listened at night to Willis Conover's jazz broadcasts on the Voice of America. After Stalin's death the door opened. In August 1956 the first Polish jazz festival took place in Sopot, and in 1958 the Jazz Jamboree began in Warsaw, one of the oldest jazz festivals in Europe. The pianist Krzysztof Komeda sought a European sound of his own, with Slavic melodies, slow tempos and plenty of space. From 1965 the record series Polish Jazz appeared on the state label Polskie Nagrania. Later the trumpeter Tomasz Stańko, the saxophonist Zbigniew Namysłowski, the violinist Zbigniew Seifert and the duo Michał Urbaniak and Urszula Dudziak also became known outside Poland. The trio of the pianist Marcin Wasilewski has continued that line since the 1990s.
genre/poolse-jazz.listen: Listen to the melody: often wistful and songlike, above a jazz rhythm.

genre/pop-uit-stockholm-max-martin.text: In Cheiron Studio in Stockholm, from the mid-1990s Max Martin and his colleagues wrote and produced the hits of the Backstreet Boys, *NSYNC and Britney Spears. Martin works with 'melodic math': lines with the same number of syllables, well-singing vowels on the high notes and a hook that often returns. Later he wrote for Taylor Swift and The Weeknd, among others.
genre/pop-uit-stockholm-max-martin.listen: ...Baby One More Time opens with three heavy piano notes and then straight away the voice: the hook is in the first seconds.

genre/popjazz-lounge-en-crime-tv-mancini.text: Henry Mancini, trained at Juilliard and for years employed by the music department of Universal, wrote the music for the TV series Peter Gunn in 1958. The cool combination of a repeated bass line, jazz horns and guitar also became a hit on record. Mancini then made the light, elegant jazz of Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), with the song ‘Moon River’, and of The Pink Panther (1963), with Plas Johnson's creeping tenor saxophone. The Argentine jazz pianist Lalo Schifrin wrote a theme in 5/4 time for Mission: Impossible (1966). This music was intended for film and television, but also for the record player at home.
genre/popjazz-lounge-en-crime-tv-mancini.listen: Notice the repeated bass line beneath a cool melody in saxophone or brass, and the 5/4 time in Schifrin.

genre/poppunk.text: Pop punk combines the speed and the guitars of punk with pop melodies and singalong choruses. In 1994 Green Day of Berkeley with Dookie and The Offspring with Smash broke through to a large audience. Around 2000 Blink-182 and many others followed, with videos full of humour on MTV.
genre/poppunk.listen: Listen to Basket Case for the fast power chords beneath a melody that you can sing along to after hearing it once.
